articles.title_orig: BACK WHEN: The world changes, people organizing for a cause does not
articles.title_zh: BACK WHEN: The world changes, people organizing for a cause does not
articles.content_orig:
Published 1:30 am Saturday, October 3, 2026
By John McNutt For Peninsula Daily News
Newspaper clipping about the law enforcement actions.
OVER THE YEARS , I have watched the world change so much. It seems that the issues of the past fade away and would not even warrant a glance today.
What we experience is normalization. Those things that were once deemed unacceptable, questionable or unethical become routine and accepted. An event in 1925 seems to show this.
On Jan. 25, 1925, a house on East Fifth Street in Port Angeles was raided by the police. The crime? A booze party. Neighbors complained that there were loud commotions and intoxicated people.
To provide some context, this incident was during the Prohibition era. There had been decades of push to prohibit the production and sale of alcohol. Many problems within our society were blamed on alcohol. Problems included alcoholism, domestic violence and political corruption. Prohibitionists viewed it as a battle for public morals and health.
The views in our society gradually changed in this regard. The Prohibition era began with the 18th Amendment to the U. S. Constitution in 1919. The Prohibition era was between 1920 and 1933. The 21st Amendment to the Constitution ended Prohibition in 1933.
The raid on this house was during a time when alcohol was still viewed as a severe detriment to society. This raid was front-page news for months.
Patrolman Norton entered the house and found 13 people. Some were intoxicated. Some were minors. Norton held them there, although some resistance was offered. Of course, the police found moonshine in the house and evidence that some of it had been poured out to avoid being taken into evidence.
Three people were arrested: Harry Malone, Howard Leigh (aka Robert Lee) and Sidney Grimes. The police were praised for breaking this up. Some neighbors viewed the house as a “tough place.” Others were afraid to let their children go out after dark.
“Grave” charges were filed against these men. They were charged with “Contributing to the delinquency of a minor female child.” At least one of the girls caught was younger than 16. Bail was set at $1,000 each ($19,000 in 2026 dollars). They could not come up with that amount of money. Seattle attorney W. G. Beardsley would represent the men.
On Feb. 3, 1925, there was a mass meeting held at the Masonic Lodge. Who should attend? Those “interested in making and keeping this community a safe place to raise girls.” Most local social and fraternal organizations were represented at this meeting.
About 1,000 people attended the meeting. There was a unanimous vote calling for a grand jury to “investigate alleged immoral conditions in the city.” They also endorsed efforts by the mayor and police to clean up crime. They also expressed fear that private citizens might take the law into their own hands.
As a result of this meeting, and after stirring speeches, a new organization was formed. It was the Public Welfare and Law Enforcement League. Their slogans would be “Militant Morality” and “Make Port Angeles a Safe Place to Raise Girls.”
It appears the community had “a spontaneous outburst of righteous wrath and indignation.” There were rumors of high school girls being involved, plus concerns about other houses hosting similar parties.
This Welfare League would be chaired by the Rev. Erle Howell. Other members included the Rev. Stuart Goude, Ida MacKechnie, Dr. W. A. Ingalls, Mrs. James Burgess, Addie Kern, Mrs. Sharenbroich, Mrs. Harry Coventon, Fred Bishop, Mrs. William Wright, Dr. Claude Porter and A. M. Anderson.
The resolution for a grand jury was warmly received by Judge John Ralston, who would take it into consideration. There would need to be a public process and a declaration of an emergency before a grand jury could be convened.
On Feb. 4, 1925, the fourth and fifth suspects, Fred Henning and Clifford Hulse, were arrested. Henning made bail. All five men entered not guilty pleas.
Meanwhile, the Public Welfare and Law Enforcement League received endorsement from the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU), the local PTA, the Philomathy Club and the Moose Lodge.
The WCTU was one of the driving forces behind Prohibition. They had a strong presence in Clallam County. The WCTU’s motto was “Agitate, Educate, Legislate.” That does not sound too much different than organizations today.
The Public Welfare and Law Enforcement League officially resolved to endorse the efforts of the mayor and police chief, and further resolved that there should be a large enough police force to cover the needs of the city. At this time, there was a chief of police and three patrolmen. This police force was too small for a town our size. At the time, the population of Port Angeles was about 7,000.
The League’s efforts helped shine a light on the size of Port Angeles’ Police Department. By 1929, the police department increased to six personnel.
In their Declaration of Principles, the League took “a stand for morality against immorality.” The League would “move forward as one fighting unit in that battle that continually wages between the forces for good and the forces for evil.”
Later, the League endorsed the promotion of healthy activities for young people to “insure the coming generation arriving at maturity with healthy minds, bodies, and morals.” Their resolution included support for a city recreation director. The League later endorsed plans for new parks and playgrounds.
Three of the five men arrested went on trial in March 1925. Harry Malone, Howard Leigh, Sidney Grimes, Fred Henning and Clifford Hulse faced the charges. Malone and Leigh were found guilty. Hulse, Henning and Grimes were acquitted.
Malone and Leigh were sentenced to eight months in jail and a $100 fine ($1,900 in 2026 dollars). The judge hoped “that the sentence would provide a lesson for the young men that they would heed and keep out of trouble in the future.”
I found nothing regarding the Public Welfare and Law Enforcement League after 1925. It seems that the indignation of the events faded over time.
In the world today, an event like this would hardly be noticed. Yet, the desire for a safe community does not fade away.
It is also important to remember that our nation and society have long endorsed and supported grassroots organizations. Some endure. Others fade away, especially after each election. Even if we do not support some organizations, we are free to start and support other organizations with opposing viewpoints.
Maybe that is democracy at work.
John McNutt is a descendant of Clallam County pioneers and treasurer of the North Olympic History Center Board of Directors. He can be reached at woodrowsilly@gmail.com .
McNutt’s Clallam history column appears the first Saturday of every month.

articles.content_orig:
Quiles heads to Japan with his first match point, but how can the #28 clinch the title this weekend?
Just 150 points remain up for grabs after Japan, and for Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team), that can only mean one thing: match point. The Spanish sensation heads to Japan with a 131-point advantage over his title rivals, giving him his first opportunity to be crowned World Champion.
Simply put, if Quiles leaves Motegi with at least a 150-point advantage, then the #28 will be crowned your 2026 Moto3 World Champion. Four riders remain in mathematical contention, with Quiles, Alvaro Carpe (Red Bull KTM Ajo), David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) and Brian Uriarte (Red Bull KTM Ajo) all facing a crucial weekend at Motegi.
If Quiles wins on Sunday and takes the maximum 25 points available, he would need Carpe to finish P10 or below, while Almansa and Uriarte would both need to finish P9 or lower. The #28 can also seal the title with a second-place finish. In that scenario, Carpe would need to finish P15 or below, with Almansa and Uriarte crossing the line P14 or lower.
Third place or lower wouldn’t be enough for Quiles to become World Champion, meaning the Moto3 title fight would continue until at least Indonesia.
It has already been an incredible season for Quiles, who has earned nine race wins and 13 podiums from the opening 15 rounds. The #28 has already scored 32 points more than his entire 2025 campaign, underlining just how impressive his form has been this year.

articles.title_orig: America Wants to Make More Generic Drugs. India Shows Why That’s Hard.
articles.title_zh: America Wants to Make More Generic Drugs. India Shows Why That’s Hard.
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s order to levy 100% tariffs on certain patented pharmaceutical products and ingredients takes effect on Tuesday.
But experts question the extent to which the move will achieve its goal of spurring more drug manufacturing in the US. That’s because the burden will fall most heavily on small and midsize companies that generally don’t have the wherewithal to shift or expand production in America.
Instead, experts say, the tariffs could force these drugmakers to close or merge with larger rivals, which could in turn reduce the number of medications that they provide to patients and could lead to higher prices – which is the last thing Trump says he wants.
What’s more, the tariffs could dampen the discovery of new medicines since these smaller firms tend to be more innovative, some experts argue.
The tariffs were announced in April, but the president had long signaled that he would target the industry, which had largely escaped such levies for decades due to a longstanding international agreement designed to keep essential medicines flowing freely across borders.
However, there are many provisions and exceptions that will limit the tariffs’ impact. Notably, the levies won’t apply to the larger pharma companies that have signed “Most Favored Nation” agreements. These manufacturers have promised to beef up their domestic production, as well as provide their medicines at lower prices to Medicaid and TrumpRx , the administration’s direct-to-consumer clearinghouse. They make the vast majority of brand-name drugs.
Also, generic medications, orphan drugs for rare diseases and certain specialty medicines are largely exempt. Patented pharmaceutical products from the European Union , Switzerland, Japan and South Korea, which have existing bilateral trade deals, will be subject to a 15% tariff rate, while those from the United Kingdom will not be subject to the levies. And companies that have an agreement to produce more in the US will face a 20% tariff.
That leaves a small share of pharmaceutical manufacturers and their products that will be subject to the 100% tariff rate, industry analysts said when the levies were unveiled.
There are more than 100 drugmakers that make at least one drug that is not exempt, according to a preliminary analysis from the Brookings Institution. A majority of these companies do not have any production facilities – instead, they use contract manufacturers to make their medications, said Marta Wosinska, a senior fellow at Brookings.
There is a “crazy level” of competition for contract manufacturing capacity in the US, so it would be very expensive for these drugmakers to make more of their products domestically, she told CNN.
“Their pockets are not as deep,” she said of the smaller companies.
Many may have no choice but to sell themselves to larger players in the industry if they can’t negotiate deals with the White House, Wosinska said.
‘Voters are like, No thanks’: Trump’s tariffs fall flat with the working class
Patients with conditions that aren’t treated by major pharmaceutical manufacturers could feel the biggest impact since they often depend on medications made by smaller companies. The prices of these medicines will likely rise, said Mollie Sitkowski, an international trade lawyer with Faegre Drinker. Plus, she expects there will be fewer new drugs released in coming years.
The Biotechnology Innovation Organization, which represents smaller and mid-sized drugmakers, wrote to the Commerce Department earlier this month warning that “tariffs that punish U.S. innovators are counterproductive and risk slowing the investment and innovation needed to be successful.”
“The reality is that tariffs on America’s medicines will raise costs, impede domestic manufacturing, and divert scarce resources away from research and development critical to maintaining American biotech leadership,” wrote John Crowley, BIO’s CEO.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Falls to Mexico in U-15 World Cup Super Round
articles.title_zh: U.S. Falls to Mexico in U-15 World Cup Super Round
articles.content_orig:
Box Score & Plays | Cumulative Stats
MÉRIDA, Mexico – The United States fell to Mexico, 7-1, in extra innings Friday night in the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) U-15 Baseball World Cup Super Round at Parque Kukulcán Alamo.
The United States moved to 3-1 in the Super Round and is tied with Japan for first place in the Super Round standings. All team records and standings can be found HERE .
Team USA took a lead three batters in but its offense was held in check for the following seven innings. The team once again rode a gem from its pitching staff, holding Mexico to one hit through the first six innings before Mexico tied the game down to its final strike in the seventh. Mexico then broke through with a late surge in extra innings.
Raylen Hunter once again paced the U.S. offense and provided half of the team’s hits in a 2-for-4 performance at the plate, while Tyler Early and Paris Head each picked up base knocks.
Nate Handley-White started for the United States and set the tone from the jump, turning in 2.1 innings while fanning four. Lathan Boddie single-handedly held Mexico’s bats at bay for a majority of the contest, as he worked 4.0 hitless innings and struck out six, including escaping a bases-loaded jam in the fifth. Early took over in the seventh and was saddled with the loss, while Head and Braylon Rogers each found some time on the bump in extras.
𝙔𝙚𝙖𝙝, 𝙋‼️ Paris Head makes the play at the hot corner. T6 | 🇺🇸 1 - 🇲🇽 0 pic.twitter.com/Ut2FJFS594
In the first, Matti Di Maggio reached base for the seventh consecutive game via walk and proceeded to jaunt his way to third after a delayed steal and a straight steal of third. Paxton Scoggin put a full-count offering in play to drive in the first run of the contest.
With runners on the corners in the third, Boddie got the call from the bullpen and pumped eight pitches–seven for strikes–to strike out the next two batters and strand a pair.
Zeroes dotted the scoreboard for the next three innings, as Boddie continued to navigate traffic on the basepaths and maneuvered a bases-loaded jam in the fifth to preserve the lead.
Down to its final strike in the seventh, Mexico’s Esteban Gallardo hit a game-tying double for Mexico’s first run of the contest, knotting the game at one apiece.
With runners automatically put on first and second per international tiebreaker rules, Mexico capitalized on the  momentum shift, stringing together a trio of hits and four walks to take a 7-1 lead.
Hunter tallied his fifth multi-hit game of the tournament.
Both Matti Di Maggio and Hunter reached base for the seventh consecutive game, while Hunter leads all players in batting average (.577) and hits (15).
The U.S. pitching staff leads the tournament with a 1.67 ERA while ranking second in strikeouts (72).
Across seven games played, the U.S. pitching staff has collected double digit strikeouts on four occasions.
The United States (6-1 overall, 3-1 Super Round) wraps up Super Round play against Japan tomorrow, October 3, at 3:00 p.m. local/5:00 p.m. ET at Parque Kukulcán Alamo in Mérida, Mexico.

articles.title_orig: Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
articles.title_zh: Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
articles.content_orig:
Two Iranian nationals charged with planning an attack against the Jewish community in northern England have appeared in a London court.
The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said on Friday that Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with “preparing to commit or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism” in Manchester “on or before” Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, which began at sundown on September 20.
After appearing in Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Saturday, the men who did not enter a plea were remanded into custody. Their next hearing is set at London’s Old Bailey court for October 23.
“It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot,” police said in a separate statement on Friday.
Details of the alleged plot have not been released, but police have confirmed its “disruption”.
Counterterrorism police said Salehi and Ahmadyan, both arrested in Manchester on September 20, allegedly tried to acquire components and equipment to make an improvised explosive device and conducted reconnaissance on potential targets for attack.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Salehi and Ahmadyan arrived in the UK on a small boat from Europe several years ago. One of the men had been granted asylum and the other had a live asylum claim, the Home Office said.
“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime,” she said in a statement.
“They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement,” she added.
Iran has denied similar accusations.
The charges come a year after two people were killed in a knife and gun attack by a British citizen of Syrian descent at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in northern Manchester on October 2, 2025.
“I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy day period has caused a great deal of concern to the Jewish community, as well as with the wider public,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said on Friday.
“It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the UK.”
Detectives said there was no connection between Friday’s charges and the suspected plot involving the RAF Fairford air base, over which a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on Thursday, according to the Reuters news agency.
Britain said Tehran had been involved in an alleged plot earlier this week targeting an airbase used by the US to launch attacks against Iran.
Iran denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford plot and said speculation would “fuel Iranophobia propaganda”.

articles.title_orig: FDA concludes investigation into Cyclospora outbreak tied to recalled Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce
articles.title_zh: FDA concludes investigation into Cyclospora outbreak tied to recalled Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce
articles.content_orig:
The Marzetti Company President and CEO Dave Ciesinski discusses how the cyclospora outbreak has affected the salad mix and dressing business and inflation on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said Friday that it concluded its investigation into the Cyclospora outbreak associated with iceberg lettuce from Mexico, finding "strong" evidence linking the infections to recalled products from Taylor Farms de Mexico.
The cyclosporiasis outbreak — one of the largest foodborne illness events in recent U.S. history — has been linked to more than 12,800 cases across 21 states and hundreds of hospitalizations.
Two related deaths have been reported in Michigan, and both people had significant underlying health conditions, according to health officials.
The outbreak prompted a massive recall by Taylor Farms de Mexico, which announced in July that it was voluntarily pulling all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from U.S. shelves.
CHILI PEPPER RECALLED AFTER VIDEO CAPTURES WOMAN'S HORRIFYING DISCOVERY INSIDE JAR
Packages of Taylor Farms salad greens are displayed at a Safeway store in Kings Beach, California, on July 16, 2026. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Following the recall, the FDA initiated onsite inspections in Mexico.
During its traceback investigation, the FDA said it identified multiple farms and a processing facility in Mexico that supplied the recalled shredded lettuce distributed by Taylor Fresh Foods.
Two environmental samples tested positive for Cyclospora, according to the FDA.
The agency said one positive sample came from a tank that held outgoing wastewater from the company's processing facility. The other was taken from a drainage ditch at an iceberg lettuce farm.
Although the FDA said it was unable to determine how the contamination transpired, the agency said the data strongly suggested that the outbreak was tied to lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico.
RECALL OF POPULAR SOFT DRINK HITS 77,000 CANS AFTER ZERO-SUGAR LABELS FOUND ON FULL-SUGAR SODA
A drone view shows the fields near the installations of U.S. supplier Taylor Farms, following the temporary closure announced by Taylor Farms, in Doctor Mora, Guanajuato state, Mexico, July 24, 2026. (REUTERS/Daniel Becerril / Reuters)
"While there is currently not enough evidence to conclusively determine how contamination occurred in this outbreak, the positive samples show that Cyclospora was present in the environment where lettuce was grown and processed," the FDA said.
"This adds to the strong epidemiological data and traceback convergence supporting the link between this outbreak and recalled shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico," the agency added.
A spokesperson for parent company Taylor Fresh Foods addressed the FDA's findings in a statement to Reuters.
"The independent grower where a positive sample was found is no longer part of our supplier program. The sample FDA referenced came from discharged waste and sewer water outside of our processing facility," the spokesperson said.
"As FDA noted in its report, there is currently not enough evidence to conclusively determine how contamination occurred or how results for these samples relate to ongoing genotyping of clinical specimens," the spokesperson continued.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
The produce section at a Publix in Miami Beach, Florida. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images / Getty Images)
FOX Business has reached out to Taylor Farms for comment.
The FDA said it is confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce linked to the outbreak is out of the U.S. market .
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) previously declared the outbreak over on Sept. 11.
Cyclospora is a single-celled parasite that can cause stomach cramps, nausea, fatigue, weight loss and other health problems, though some infected people remain asymptomatic, according to the CDC.

articles.title_orig: Rio Ngumoha hails Jude Bellingham as world’s best midfielder and vows to follow his path to England stardom
articles.title_zh: Rio Ngumoha hails Jude Bellingham as world’s best midfielder and vows to follow his path to England stardom
articles.content_orig:
Rio Ngumoha believes Jude Bellingham is the best midfielder in the world and hopes to follow his example in becoming an England regular.
Ngumoha made his competitive debut for England during the 2-0 win over Czechia on Tuesday night, becoming the third-youngest footballer to feature for the Three Lions in a competitive game.
Wayne Rooney and Bellingham are the only players to have achieved the feat at a younger age, with Bellingham substituted on alongside Ngumoha in midweek.
Ngumoha hailed Bellingham as the best midfielder in the world right now and hopes he can follow in the Real Madrid star's footsteps to become a regular.
At 23, Bellingham has already won 58 caps for England at senior level and has already represented the Three Lions at four major tournaments.
In June, he became the youngest player to reach 50 caps for England and ended the 2026 World Cup with seven goals, the outright most ever by an England player in a single World Cup finals.
"Jude is 23, I think, and already he's probably the best midfielder in the world at this point," Ngumoha told ITV Sport ahead of Saturday's clash with Croatia.
"He definitely believed that he would play in an England shirt at 17, same as Wayne Rooney, what he's done for his club and his country, hopefully I can do the same. It's going to be a good journey, I think."

articles.title_orig: Dad with MS targets half marathon world record
articles.title_zh: Dad with MS targets half marathon world record
articles.content_orig:
A man from Liverpool has set himself the challenge of breaking a Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon run by a man with multiple sclerosis (MS).
Father-of-two David Price, 42, was diagnosed with MS in 2018 after starting to struggle with his balance and peripheral vision.
Eight years on, Price is preparing to attempt the record at the Manchester Half Marathon, but admits to feeling nervous.
The current record is held by Chris White, who achieved a time of 1 hour 30 minutes and 46 seconds in Brighton in March this year.
"It would mean the world to me to break the record," David said. "I'm not underestimating how much of a challenge it will be, but it would be absolutely fantastic."
David, who works in IT, said his symptoms of MS first became noticeable in the office.
"I was stumbling around the office and knocking things off desks. My peripheral vision and senses had gone a little bit strange and weird," he said, adding that he also "started to get tingling arms and legs."
David described his diagnosis of MS as a "shock to the system", and something that took a long time to come to terms with.
"Me and the wife didn't have a clue what multiple sclerosis was," David recalled.
"It took me about three years to accept I had this long-term disability."
Despite medication, life has its daily challenges.
"You will have times where your cognitive functions aren't quite right or your thought process isn't quite where it should be.
"Like when you try to speak. You know what you want to say, but you struggle to get it out."
In 2021, David started to run and lift weights, something he said brought out a "remarkable" change in him.
"I never looked back from that point," he said. "I changed my mindset."
Training for Sunday's race, David said he has been listening to his body closely.
"I've got to accept that just because it's on the training plan, doesn't mean it has to be done.
"I've got to be big enough to say I'm not capable of doing that today - I need to take a rest day.'"
He said he wanted to attempt the world record to show others that setting high goals is possible.
"I'm not defined by MS," he said.
"And MS doesn't define me."
The Manchester Half Marathon takes place on Sunday 4 October.

articles.title_orig: World in Brief: G7 to release oil reserves; America’s hiring slows
articles.title_zh: World in Brief: G7 to release oil reserves; America’s hiring slows
articles.content_orig:
Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.
The French President, Emmanuel Macron , said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.
Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.
Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.
The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.
Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.
Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.
He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.
“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.
Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.
The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.
The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.
In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.
The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September.
The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.
after newsletter promotion
In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.
The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.
Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.
Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.
“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.
“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.
The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
articles.title_zh: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
articles.content_orig:
Pyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZ
North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, ⁠a day ​after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s ⁠coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been ​a ballistic missile and appeared to have come ‌down, warning ships to take ‌precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, ​issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured ⁠three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches ​across the Korean peninsula.
The missile ​test might be an attempt ​by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, ​said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president ‌at the Sejong ​Institute in Seoul, ​a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

articles.title_orig: Norfolk speedway set me on path to world title
articles.title_zh: Norfolk speedway set me on path to world title
articles.content_orig:
The newly-crowned world champion of speedway has credited his home county club with setting him on the path to success.
Norwich-born Robert Lambert, 28, lifted the trophy after winning the final Grand Prix of the season in Torun, Poland, on Saturday.
He first began riding professionally in the UK for King's Lynn Stars in Norfolk as a teen, having initially honed his craft in Germany.
"King's Lynn has been a massive, massive part of my career," he told BBC Look East presenter Amelia Reynolds.
"To race in the UK is completely different to racing in Europe - the tracks are much different, the atmosphere and pressure is much different.
"So, really, it was the building blocks to where I am today."
He said the world title was still sinking in. Walking into his living room the day after the race and seeing the trophy there was "pretty incredible".
"It's something that I'd never really believed would happen," he added.
"Obviously, you're always trying to fight to be world champion and it's always a massive dream of any kind of athlete.
"For it to come true is completely unbelievable."
But Lambert grew up with speedway and had wanted to be world champion from a very young age.
His dad, Paul, rode for Mildenhall Tigers, and Robert became its club mascot at around the same time his mum Helen got his first motorbike, aged three.
A profile in the Fen Tigers programme from when he was five years old said he was on the go "constantly" and could not wait to get home from Bawdeswell Primary School so he could practise his skids with his dad.
It adds: "Robert's ambition is to be world speedway champion one day."
At the tender age of six, he was competing in grass track.
He first rode for King's Lynn Young Stars in 2013 before stepping up to the top flight a year later, as a 16-year-old.
He said as a young lad, he was ribbed by team "veterans" and other riders in the league, which helped him toughen up.
"In turn it made me a lot stronger for the future, until I kind of gained some respect from them that I can be a good rider and to give them a good challenge," he explained.
He rode for King's Lynn until the Covid-19 pandemic and moved on to racing in Europe, returning to the Stars for a brief spell in the 2023 season.
Lambert said many riders from his past had been in touch to congratulate him.
"My phone has been on fire since Sunday," he added.
"It has been so incredible to have such a great support.
"[I've heard from] people who were helping me at the beginning and other colleagues and riders who I haven't spoken to for a while."
While he may be forgiven for taking some time out and bathing in the glory, Lambert said he would not be sitting on his laurels.
With his ambition fulfilled, he now wants "multiple" world titles.
"I'm still very young and and I believe I've still got a lot to learn in the sport of speedway."

articles.title_orig: Russia leads world in cat ownership — yet has 2.8 million strays
articles.title_zh: Russia leads world in cat ownership — yet has 2.8 million strays
articles.content_orig:
Russia has the highest rate of cat ownership in the world, with nearly 59% of households keeping at least one cat — and an estimated 2.8 million stray cats living on its streets, a number that rose sharply after the 2022 mobilisation order sent thousands of pet owners fleeing the country or to the front amid Russia's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine.
According to a 2024-2026 study by analytics platform Seasia Stats, Russia ranks first globally for cats as pets. Romania ranks second in Europe at 48%, followed by Poland at 41%, Latvia at 37% and Hungary at 35%.
Outside Europe, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, New Zealand and the US also make the top 10. The Seasia Stats findings are consistent with a 2023 study by insurer Ingosstrakh and the Financial University, in which 58.8% of Russian respondents described themselves as cat owners.
The stray figures come from a separate study by the Centre for Animal Nutrition and Well-being Studies, the Nika animal charity and research firm Ipsos.
They put the total stray animal population in Russia in 2025 at nearly 3.6 million, of which 2.8 million are cats and 800,000 are dogs.
Of those, around 170,000 were in shelters at the time of the study, while the rest were living on the streets. Researchers say up to 98% of stray cats and dogs were once domestic pets abandoned by their owners.
Animal welfare organisations recorded a sharp increase in abandonments after Russia announced partial mobilisation in September 2022.
Men who received call-up papers were either leaving the country or preparing for deployment and in many cases could not arrange care for their animals or find shelter places.
On classified advertising websites, owners threatened to have pets put down if no one took them. Shelter volunteers reported similar ultimatums from people surrendering animals in person.
Russia has 819 shelters, the overwhelming majority privately run, alongside hundreds of charities and tens of thousands of volunteers. Together they care for between 170,000 and 250,000 animals — no more than 5–7% of the estimated stray population.
The popularity of cats in Eastern Europe has historical roots: before industrialised agriculture, cats served a practical function on farms, where their presence and scent deterred rodents.
In Southeast Asia, researchers link rising ownership to urbanisation and the growth of a middle class.
Cats have lived alongside humans for around 10,000 years. Today, they are human companions of choice, alongside dogs.

articles.title_orig: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
articles.title_zh: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
articles.content_orig:
As the AI boom becomes a major part of political debate, the public backlash against data centers in the U.S. is spreading to Europe and Asia — raising risks for investors.
Across the Atlantic, negative sentiment is growing in Europe, which has more at stake due to its densely populated countries and higher electricity prices , experts told CNBC.
Similar tensions are emerging in South Korea, with growing opposition to data centers near residential areas and proposals for tighter local restrictions, even as the national government pushes to accelerate development.
Public opposition has already impacted around $42 billion of data center investments in Europe, in account delays and cancellations, according to research from STL Partners. That compares to around $77 billion in the U.S.
The pushback could be the "straw that breaks the camel's back," Olivier Darmouni, associate professor at HEC Paris who specializes in the energy transition, told CNBC.
More than 70 data center projects in Europe were rejected or restricted between January and April — more than in all of 2025, according to the European Data Center Monitor. It found that pushback had snowballed from local town halls to courts, regulators and parliaments.
Scotland has paused planning approvals for new hyperscale data centers after campaigners called on the government to avoid the "cautionary tale" of Ireland, where overwhelming power demand led to a moratorium.
Constraints have been rising in the Nordics, where investors were drawn to large tracts of land and renewable energy. After a surge in power applications , Denmark passed an emergency law that could see data centers at the back of the queue for grid power applications.
Spain also proposed new data center rules this summer, requiring data centers to source 80% of their electricity from renewables. Projects in the U.K. have stalled after pushback from locals.
Much of the concern centers around water usage , power consumption , electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. There is also little agreement on how many permanent jobs the sector creates, and no precedent for projecting a center's economic value per megawatt.
"The gains of AI are very diffused," Darmouni told CNBC.
"There's definitely been more understanding of the scale of the potential AI build-out and its geographical spread, and perhaps ... more information about how much bigger these are, and that they're a little bit more like giant ghost warehouses that consume a lot of resources and can hurt local communities in some ways."
Europe's denser population, and the fact that many data center operators are U.S. companies, might mean that the backlash hits harder, the professor added.
South Korea, home to tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, sits at the heart of the AI supply chain. In June, its government named AI data centers as one of three major investment projects, alongside semiconductors and physical AI.
But its push to build the infrastructure needed is running into resistance at the local level.
In the Geumcheon district of southwestern Seoul, residents have called for authorities to revoke the building permit and halt construction of a data center near their homes, according to the local government.
In July, officials announced plans to require consent from a majority of residents living within 200 meters of proposed data center sites and to introduce a three-stage system for reviewing projects and mediating disputes.
Residents have also gathered outside the local government office on weekday mornings for months to protest against the project. The demonstrations had continued for 172 days as of mid-August, according to local media .
In Gwacheon, a city just south of Seoul, a local council member proposed an ordinance aimed at protecting nearby residents from risks associated with data centers operating around the clock, including potential fires involving backup batteries.
Despite the pusback, the AI boom shows little sign of slowing down.
But a community's ability "to derail a $10 billion [data center] plan is quite powerful," said Asya Walters, managing director at Alvarez & Marsal.
She told CNBC the business-friendly environment in the U.S. has historically made it easier to overcome pushback.
But in Europe and Asia, there's some "hot and coldness" at the country level about where demand is going, Walters said. The "push and pull" between favorable conditions for data centers and more restrictive regulation can be challenging for investment.
Public backlash can also end up raising costs for operators, because even if they pull out of a project before construction starts, money will likely have already been spent.
Though most capex expenditure happens after the permits are in place, operators spend a lot to reach that point, "so there is some loss that could happen there if they never get the permits," Walters said.
"Digital infrastructure is becoming more visible and it's understandable that communities want to understand what's being built near them, why it's needed and how local impacts are being managed," said Eulalia Flo, vice president of growth and emerging markets, EMEA at Equinix , one of the biggest data center operators in Europe.
"We don't see this as a structural constraint on growth, but the policy environment is genuinely tightening in some markets," said Flo.
But the AI buildout has meant "a misunderstanding of the industry in a very broad sense," according to Dominic Ward, CEO of data center operator Verne.
"We used to be a completely unknown part of the economy," Ward told CNBC. "We were just a black box. We were just a building that had stuff that went in that nobody understood. Now we are one of the fundamental layers driving the economy."
He added: "Now everybody knows where they are, so there's kind of no hiding behind this."

articles.title_orig: ‘Can’t Get Much Bigger Than This,’ ‘GOAT’s HOME’ – Sports World Buzzes as Caitlin Clark Joins College GameDay’s 1st Iowa Visit in 20 Years for Ohio State Clash
articles.title_zh: ‘Can’t Get Much Bigger Than This,’ ‘GOAT’s HOME’ – Sports World Buzzes as Caitlin Clark Joins College GameDay’s 1st Iowa Visit in 20 Years for Ohio State Clash
articles.content_orig:
Caitlin Clark is heading back to Iowa City, and she is doing it for one of the biggest football weekends the Hawkeye community has seen in years. The Fever star will serve as the celebrity guest picker on ESPN's College GameDay when No. 14 Iowa hosts No. 5 Ohio State on Saturday.
Clark's appearance comes days after her WNBA season ended with Indiana Fever's playoff loss to the Las Vegas Aces, giving the Iowa legend a chance to return home almost immediately. Needless to say, the CC fanbase was hyped by the news.
ESPN's College GameDay announced Clark's appearance Friday evening, calling her a "Hawkeye legend" and confirming that she will join the crew for Saturday's broadcast in Iowa City.
As a guest picker, Clark will give her own predictions for the day's marquee matchup alongside the GameDay panel.
The show begins at 9 a.m. ET and runs until 12 p.m. ET, with the GameDay set at the Pentacrest. The football game between Iowa and Ohio State is scheduled for 3:30 p.m. ET.
Clark will join a stacked GameDay panel featuring Rece Davis, Kirk Herbstreit, Desmond Howard, Nick Saban, Pete Thamel, and Pat McAfee. The visit is also a notable one for the show itself, as this will be College GameDay's third football trip to Iowa City.
READ MORE: 'Biggest Screw Job in WNBA History,' 'Ridiculous' — Dave Portnoy, Hoops World Sound Off As Refs Overlook Bleeding Caitlin Clark As Fever Get Eliminated
The announcement immediately sent Iowa fans into a frenzy.
Hawkeye insider David Eickholt summed up the excitement simply, writing , "Can't get much bigger than this."
Barstool Iowa kept its reaction shorter, proclaiming , "GOATS HOME."
247Sports' Eliot Clough also felt the energy building, acknowledging , "That's a big one. Caitlin Clark mania is returning back to Iowa City."
Another Clark supporter pointed out that the timing could hardly be better. Nike's three-day Caitlin 1 pop-up block party is running in downtown Iowa City through Saturday, right near the Pentacrest, where GameDay is set up, making her guest-picker appearance feel like a natural fit for a weekend already centered on her.
"I had guessed this and she may have done it even had they won last night. The crossover promotion is just too good with her big shoe event in Iowa City extending thru Saturday," the fan wrote .
"The opportunity to do College Gameday and drop in on her shoe celly is simply too perfect to pass up. Gonna be a zoo there tomorrow and lord do I wish I were there."
Hawkeye Sports columnist Chad Leistikow made clear that Clark's presence takes an already major weekend to another level entirely, commenting, "The weekend in Iowa City just got even bigger."
Another reaction came from former UNCO point guard Molly McGrath, who wrote , "The rumors are true!!!!"
One excited CC fan simply posted , "Omggggggg."
Clark's return carries plenty of meaning for Iowa fans. She led the Hawkeyes to back-to-back national championship games and became one of the biggest stars in college basketball before entering the WNBA.
Iowa announced in 2024 that it would retire Clark's No. 22, and she finished her college career as the NCAA Division I scoring record holder for men's or women's basketball.
Now, she gets to return to the place where that rise began for another major Iowa sporting event.
Clark's visit to Iowa lines up perfectly with Nike's launch of the Caitlin 1. The shoe officially launched Oct. 1 and is being rolled out in roughly 5,000 stores, reportedly giving it the largest retail footprint for a Nike Basketball signature debut.
MORE: 'Worst Coach I've Ever Seen,' 'Never the Right Fit' — Calls Mount To Fire Stephanie White After Caitlin Clark, Fever's Playoffs Exit
The Caitlin 1 pop-up block party in downtown Iowa City is also running through Oct. 3.
So while Iowa prepares for one of its biggest football games of the season, Clark has plenty going on around it. The Fever star gets to return to her old college home, soak in the buzz around her first Nike signature shoe, and pick a winner on College GameDay.
And judging by the early reaction, Iowa City is more than ready to have its Hawkeye legend back home.
This article originally appeared on Pro Football Network .

articles.title_orig: DA did not review witness statements and other evidence Cornell police collected in alleged gang rape of student
articles.title_zh: DA did not review witness statements and other evidence Cornell police collected in alleged gang rape of student
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University police spoke to witnesses and received anonymous tips about an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house in the first weeks of its investigation two years ago , but the local prosecutor did not review the additional information before deciding not to bring charges.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said he based his decision not to pursue charges on the accuser’s initial six-page statement given to police.
Investigators from the campus police department documented those witness interviews and other steps taken to determine whether Jane Doe, a 20-year-old woman who reported the incident, was the victim of sexual assault during a party at the Chi Phi house from Oct. 19 to 20, 2024, according police records obtained by NBC News.
Documents reviewed by NBC News offer the most thorough look to date at how police handled the allegations from Jane Doe, who last month filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and seven Chi Phi brothers who she alleges sexually assaulted her over the course of hours while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.
Van Houten, along with police and university officials, has come under intense fire for their handling of the matter. Jane Doe’s attorney has argued that she was failed by authorities who did not conduct a thorough investigation and who prejudged the events based on her earlier statement that she consented to parts of the night.
Gov. Kathy Hochul on Thursday announced the appointment of Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to consider whether charges are appropriate.
“In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript” of the victim’s interview, Hochul asked Friday at a news conference announcing James’s appointment.
On Nov. 25, 2024, a police investigator approached Van Houten’s office to tell them about interviews they’d done.
An investigator in Van Houten’s office, according to the documents, replied that “he and several [attorneys] at the District Attorney’s Office had read [Jane Doe’s] statement … [and] stated that they all agreed that, based on [Jane Doe’s] statement, criminal charges would not be pursued in this case.”
Van Houten defended his decision Monday and said that Jane Doe’s statement did not allege criminality. He also agreed to reopen his inquiry before that role was assigned to the attorney general.
When reached for comment by email Friday, Van Houten argued “there was nothing to review” in that discussion with police because the interviews flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.”
Van Houten did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.
The records also show that police were receiving fragments of a larger Snapchat thread where one member of the group announced there was “free p----” in the alumni room of the house, where Jane Doe engaged in what she said was initially a consensual threesome.
“Similarly there was no material obtained by CUPD from Snapchat (what was provided came from a witness),” Van Houten added. “So again nothing to review.”
It was unclear whether Van Houten was aware that on Nov. 26, 2024, police made a request to Snapchat for a more complete data history.
That request was answered on Dec. 23, when police said they obtained 1,665 pieces of data from five Snapchat accounts.
“After reviewing all of the data returned from Snapchat, there appeared to be only 3 snapchats that included [Jane Doe] or mentioned this incident,” a CUPD investigator wrote. “None of these 3 snapchats show anything that can be construed as being criminal in nature. No further action taken.”
Jane Doe was only notified by Cornell police about the district attorney’s Nov. 25 determination not to pursue charges nearly two months later on, Jan. 21, 2025.
Van Houten added that his office had “no part in the timing” of conveying his decision to Jane Doe, who was never interviewed by his office.
Thomas Giuffra, the attorney representing Jane Doe, learned about that delay from NBC News’ request for comment Friday. He said that his client — during that two-month window — believed “they were still investigating.”
“I was unaware that they had made the decision to not prosecute in November,” Giuffra said. “If so, that is worse than I thought.”
If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.
Shayna Jacobs is a national reporter for NBC News digital.
Kenzi Abou-Sabe is a reporter and producer in the NBC News Investigative Unit.

articles.title_orig: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.title_zh: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.content_orig:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.
It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.
Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".
Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."
"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.
"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."
Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.
Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".
Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.
The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday .
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title_orig: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
articles.title_zh: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
articles.content_orig:
Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election
S hortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.
“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.
Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.
On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.
Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.
Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro , 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.
“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum , is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.
“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.
Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs ” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land .
While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.
Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth , but it is currently at a low point , with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.
“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”
A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.
At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.
Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.
“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.
“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.
As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved , others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.
Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen , and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.
Many therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from a simple transfer of his father’s voter base and from an anti-Lula vote .
“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.
Actor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed by Jair Bolsonaro’s election that she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.
She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.
She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.
“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.

articles.content_orig:
Search across reports, market insights, and blog stories.
China is unlikely to significantly increase its crude oil imports through the remainder of the year, according to OilPrice, as prices have climbed back above $100 per barrel and independent refiners face difficulty securing cheaper supply following the near-disappearance of Iranian barrels.
September import volumes are expected to be roughly in line with August levels, continuing a pattern of recovering shipments. The cargoes arriving in September were purchased when oil prices were in the $80s, before the latest escalation in early September pushed and held Brent above $100 per barrel.
China's crude oil imports rose for a second straight month in August, as refiners sought additional non-Middle Eastern supply and increased overseas fuel shipments amid eased export restrictions. The August level remained 23.4% below the same month a year earlier, though it marked a clear improvement from the June low of 7.1 million barrels per day.
China cut total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, capping three months of very low import levels driven by high prices and constrained Middle Eastern supply.
The outlook for the rest of the year has weakened as oil trades above $100 per barrel again and a U.S. blockade effectively removes the regular cheap supply that China's independent refiners relied on for years to stay competitive. The teapots could begin reducing refinery processing rates as prices rise and supply from major exporters such as Venezuela and Iran dries up due to U.S. foreign policy decisions.
Chinese state giants are also not rushing to buy much higher crude volumes above $100 a barrel with record-high freight costs, according to analysts. Samuel Kong, senior oil analyst at FGE NexantECA, told Bloomberg that significant upside to China's crude imports is not expected, partly because hefty premiums and expensive freight raise feedstock costs and erode margins.
Analysts at FGE NexantECA and Energy Aspects have revised down their earlier fourth-quarter projections for China's crude oil imports by about 400,000 barrels per day. These consultancies now expect China's crude oil imports to reach 9.2 million to 9.3 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, well below last year's average of 11.6 million barrels per day.

articles.title_orig: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.title_zh: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.content_orig:
Nick Neville , Community Correspondent , Orlando, FL
KISSIMMEE, Fla. – A now former vendor at Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks says she was forced out of the space she rented for about a decade, triggering a viral backlash and calls online for a boycott of the food truck park.
Gabriella Santos, who operated Los Cipotes, posted a video saying she was given just hours to move her food truck after ten years at the location. The post drew millions of views and sparked a heated debate on social media.
Santos told News 6 that her frustration built for years, citing what she describes as safety concerns, rising operating costs, and feeling unsupported.
She also said vendors paid out of pocket for events, absorbed new fees, and saw sales decline as more trucks were added to the park.
“Somebody’s making that extra money, and it’s not us,” Santos said in a Friday interview.
Santos said a lease renewal meeting this week became a boiling point. She claims a manager asked for access to her point-of-sale system, which she believes was framed as a way to determine rent.
“She said wanted access to the POS, and I said ‘Why do you need access to that?’” Santos said. “’Oh it’s because that’s how we’re going to balance how much your rent is going to be.’”
Santos also raised concerns about what she says were new lease terms, including language she interpreted as requiring 60 percent if a renewed lease was later broken.
World Food Trucks publicly disputed that claim, saying in a social media response: “That claim is completely false.”
Santos later clarified during the interview that she was describing her perception of what the changes would mean for her business, not alleging a literal demand for 60 percent of sales.
“I never said that,” she said. “What I said was that they wanted 60 percent of my business because that’s how I feel. That’s my personal feeling of what you’re doing to me. You’re taking my profits.”
She told News 6 she understand the terms to mean the food truck park would have wanted 60 percent of the remainder of the lease agreement.
Santos said after refusing to sign the new lease, she was told to leave by midnight on Thursday. Photos obtained by News 6 show her former spot is now surrounded by tables.
In a statement to News 6, World Food Trucks said in part, “We respect every vendor’s right to share their experience. We also believe disagreements deserve respectful conversation and accurate information. Our vendors pay a fixed weekly rent, rather than a percentage of their food sales, and we remain committed to clear communication with our vendor community.
Our focus is on supporting the more than 100 businesses that make World Food Trucks possible. We invite everyone to visit, meet the people behind the food, and support the local entrepreneurs who have helped build this community.”
Santos said she believes the viral reaction resonated because people see small business owners as vulnerable.
She said she is speaking for other vendors who are too afraid to go public.
“I think people don’t want little people to get bullied,” she said.

articles.title_orig: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.title_zh: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination” .
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates , where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”
