articles.title_orig: US job growth undershoots expectations in September, but labor market remains stable
articles.title_zh: US job growth undershoots expectations in September, but labor market remains stable
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Employment in the United States grew by 29,000 jobs in September, missing analysts' expectations significantly, with the unemployment rate rising slightly to 4.2 percent, government data showed on Friday.
Adding to the weak data, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) also revised down job figures for July and August by a combined 60,000 jobs, the department said in a statement.
The revision to July's data showed that the world's largest economy lost jobs that month, as opposed to posting a gain of 21,000 as previously reported.
The data comes ahead of key midterm elections in November where President Donald Trump's Republican Party is facing a stern test over his handling of the economy.
Trump's top economic advisor Kevin Hassett said he was "not even a little bit" disappointed in Friday's data.
Analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires and the Wall Street Journal had expected the US economy to add 84,000 jobs in September.
Employment in most major sectors was largely unchanged, the BLS reported, with health care posting gains of 17,000.
The sector has propped up the labor market in the United States in the last year, as an aging population requires more care.
September's sector gains were slower than its average monthly gain of 33,000 over the last year.
"With... immigrant labor losing their status to work in the US, that restriction in labor supply is causing subdued labor growth now for health care," said Ken Kim, senior economist at KPMG.
The financial sector continued its downward slide, bringing its overall slump from a recent peak in May 2025 to 129,000.
Average hourly earnings for all employees were up 3.0 percent year-on-year, with wages continuing to lag behind stubbornly high inflation -- meaning most workers are seeing real wage losses.
"It does have a big impact on households, that's why consumer confidence has been tanking," KPMG's Kim told AFP. "Because it's corrosive, (with) cumulative inflation."
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren seized on the data to criticize Trump's performance.
"Since the start of Trump's war, real wages have fallen 0.7 percent as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up," she said, referring to the US war against Iran launched in late February.
The conflict has plunged the Middle East into violence and sent global energy prices skyrocketing, as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's regional allies and choked a key trading route.
The data comes after the US Federal Reserve -- which has a dual mandate to maintain inflation at a long-term two-percent target while ensuring maximum employment -- raised interest rates last month to address high prices.
The US labor market has been largely in balance this year, with modest job gains and a steady unemployment rate.
That steadiness has allowed the Fed to focus on the inflation side of its mandate. Raising interest rates tends to cool inflation but can also limit economic activity, which can affect the job market.
This week, two key Fed policymakers indicated that the central bank may not raise rates again at its October meeting, although markets continue to expect a further hike before the end of the year.
Friday's jobs data "lends support to the less hawkish Fed officials that indicate no need to rush and deliver the next rate hike at the end of this month," said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.
Nancy Vanden Houten at Oxford Economics disagreed, expecting upside risks to inflation to continue to dominate Fed policymakers' thinking and to see them raise rates again.
KPMG's Kim stressed that Friday's data was not positive for many households.
"Even though today's numbers were good for the market in terms of the Fed not having to hike rates, the wages (data) suggests that households are falling behind against inflation," he said.

articles.title_orig: US arrests tech CEO accused of smuggling $300M in Nvidia chips into China
articles.title_zh: US arrests tech CEO accused of smuggling $300M in Nvidia chips into China
articles.content_orig:
The US has arrested another suspect accused of smuggling high-end computer servers containing export-controlled Nvidia chips into China.
In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Justice accused 38-year-old Greg Lui of using false paperwork to mask shipments of servers worth more than $300 million that he allegedly knew were ultimately destined for China.
As the CEO of Earthmade Computer, Lui allegedly conspired with freight-forwarding firms in South Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore to illegally divert chip shipments into China, including Nvidia’s A100 GPUs and H100 GPUs, the FBI’s indictment alleged. These are not Nvidia’s most advanced chips. However, the chips can process large amounts of data and train large language models, which the US fears could pose national security risks if China suddenly gets access to enough chips to drastically advance its AI or strengthen its military.
Emails and bank records exposed the smuggling scheme, the DOJ alleged, which started in October 2023 and continued until August 2026.
One key piece of evidence is a 2024 email discussing an order for 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs that were fraudulently claimed as destined for Malaysia. After “Lui submitted a purchase order to a US manufacturer for 27 of these servers for approximately $7,614,000,” the DOJ alleged that a co-conspirator told a Malaysian government official that all 27 were shipped to China.
A similar shipment of 92 export-controlled servers was allegedly routed through Singapore to Malaysia, then Hong Kong. Finally, the chips went to a Chinese firm based in Hangzhou, the FBI alleged, which The Wall Street Journal last year described as China’s AI hub.
Yet another flagged 2024 shipment shows how far Lui allegedly went to fool US officials.
When shipping 100 Malaysian-bound servers—each containing Nvidia H100 GPUs worth over $22 million—Lui allegedly submitted fraudulent documentation from a fake buyer identifying its CEO as “Jackie Lui.” Three years prior, Lui “purchased the identifying documents of an individual whose identity is known to the grand jury and used this identity to conduct business transactions in furtherance of the export evasion scheme,” the FBI alleged.
In 2024, Lui’s firm allegedly received more than $176 million from the scheme. Payment records from Lui’s accounts with Bank of America and JP Morgan provided further evidence of how he allegedly operated the smuggling business.
Arguing the evidence backs the charges, the DOJ wants to seize all funds gained through the scheme. Arrested on three counts, Lui is accused of conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, as well as federal smuggling and money laundering laws. He faces up to 20 years in prison if found guilty of either the conspiracy or money laundering counts, and the smuggling charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 10 years.
Lui’s arrest comes after an Nvidia senior manager based in Taiwan was linked to a similar smuggling scheme allegedly run by ex-Supermicro staff in that country.
At that time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged Supermicro to fix its compliance problem while claiming there was no evidence of smuggling. Since then, as more arrests have followed, Nvidia has pivoted from denying smuggling to downplaying the role smuggled chips and servers play in China’s AI industry, which is now largely powered by Huawei chips. On Thursday, a spokesperson told Bloomberg that “less than one half of one percent to Nvidia products” have allegedly been diverted to China.
“Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has,” Nvidia’s spokesperson said.
Experts suggest that the black market is “hard to measure,” though, and likely much bigger than has been reported.
Increasingly, Nvidia faces questions about its own “blind spots” when it comes to compliance with export controls, according to a lengthy Bloomberg investigation “based on conversations with dozens of people across five countries.”
Officials around the world suspect that hundreds of thousands of AI chips are being exchanged in a sprawling shadow trade likely powering small data centers and potentially even “a handful of hyperscalers” in China. These chips could fill a hardware gap that China doesn’t expect to address on its own until 2030, one “top executive” told Bloomberg.
Rushing to cut off the supply, US officials want Nvidia to voluntarily tighten its protocols and flag more suspicious shipments. That way, the chips don’t end up going to leading Chinese firms that Donald Trump has accused of stealing US technology to quickly expand Chinese AI capabilities, like DeepSeek.
“Government officials and industry experts are increasingly pointing to gaps in Nvidia’s due diligence, questioning how the company failed to catch red flags,” Bloomberg reported. Officials suggested the most scrutinized shipments ought to be facilities in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore.
Nvidia screens buyers and has blocked shipments when end buyers are unknown, but it’s not detecting seemingly obvious fraudulent shipments that some US officials think could easily be flagged.
For example, Nvidia and Supermicro visited a Taiwanese facility that bought high-end chips that were quickly passed on to a Chinese firm. Eventually, Taiwan’s Coast Guard “noticed discrepancies in shipping manifests,” Bloomberg reported, and seized the bulk of export-controlled servers. However, the FBI alleged that Nvidia could’ve stopped the shipments before they started since the facility “was clearly insufficient to house all the ordered servers.” Instead of exercising “basic scrutiny,” both chipmakers authorized the deal anyway, Bloomberg reported. Even more alarming, in another case, Nvidia didn’t notice that a small data center in Thailand diverting chips was relying on fake leases to purchase bulk orders. Nvidia won’t comment on whether that site was ever visited, Bloomberg noted.
Nvidia disagrees that it could’ve thwarted shipments officials have flagged. A spokesperson told Bloomberg that “a startup’s growth plan in a friendly nation is an opportunity for America, not a ‘red flag’ to be feared.” Most likely, Nvidia won’t turn down orders that don’t seem to fit existing facilities, since “Nvidia-powered servers are financeable asset that help startups secure capital and infrastructure, including data center space,” the spokesperson said.
Most glaringly, Nvidia continues to work with at least one entity that the US has recently flagged as potentially evading export curbs. Nvidia told Bloomberg it wouldn’t comment on whether it has conducted the urgent checks the US government requested to ensure Megaspeed wasn’t diverting tens of thousands of excess AI chips into China. The company will keep working with Megaspeed until it’s ordered to stop, the spokesperson said.
“When the law is clear, American companies honor US laws as they are, not as America’s critics wish they were,” Nvidia’s spokesperson said.
Rather than scrutinize its customers’ orders in countries neighboring China, Nvidia chose instead to make “an internal whitelist of Asian firms pre-approved for AI chip purchases,” sources told Bloomberg.
Overall, Bloomberg’s report suggested that unless the US specifically bans sales or requires actions, Nvidia will continue doing business that ensures its AI chips dominate the market and power the world’s leading AI models.
Stricter rules are unlikely to follow, despite some calls in Congress to pass laws cutting off China from more chips. Industry opposition already watered down one anti-smuggling bill, Bloomberg noted, and Huang recently snubbed a congressional invitation to testify on the problem.
Additionally, Huang’s growing influence over Trump has spurred the president to similarly relax more export controls . So far, the Trump administration has been happy to let Nvidia poli

articles.title_orig: AI competition between the US and China: US Rep. Khanna's 5-pillar proposal to mitigate the risks
articles.title_zh: AI competition between the US and China: US Rep. Khanna's 5-pillar proposal to mitigate the risks
articles.content_orig:
To prevent an uncontrolled AI competition US Rep. Ro Khanna calls for a US–China AI treaty
To prevent an uncontrolled  US–China AI competition, US Representative Ro Khanna, the ranking member of the House Select Committee on China, proposes a binding, enforceable and verifiable US–China AI treaty centred on managing the most extreme risks associated with advanced AI .
The proposal comes as Washington and Beijing have already begun establishing channels for dialogue on AI. During their September summit, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to create a mechanism for communication on AI-related issues and risks. Chinese officials have also publicly stressed the need to keep AI under human control, while the two governments continue to compete over advanced computing, models, semiconductors and technological capabilities.
In a commentary published on 2 October, US Representative Ro Khanna argues that Washington and Beijing “cannot afford an AI arms race” if increasingly capable systems could create risks that neither government can reliably control. US–China AI competition over artificial intelligence is increasingly being framed not only as a contest over technological leadership, but also as a potential governance and security problem.
Against this backdrop, Khanna argues that dialogue alone would not be sufficient to avoid the risk associated with this on AI competition. He proposes five pillars for a future treaty.
First, a global pause on recursive self-improvement. Khanna calls for restrictions on systems capable of designing, testing and improving AI systems with limited or no human intervention. The concern is that recursive improvement could accelerate AI capabilities faster than existing safeguards can keep pace, creating a need for international limits on this form of AI autonomy.
Second, a global pause on superintelligence. Khanna proposes that the US and China jointly halt the development of systems that exceed human capabilities across essentially all domains until adequate safeguards are established. While the definition and measurement of superintelligence remain contested, the proposal would shift regulation from specific AI applications toward the development of frontier capabilities themselves.
Third, kill switches for advanced AI models. Khanna calls for mechanisms that would allow advanced systems to be disabled if they behave unpredictably or pose a serious threat. While experts disagree over how effective such mechanisms would be, he presents them as an additional layer of control rather than a standalone safety measure.
Fourth, mandatory testing in air-gapped environments before release. AI models would undergo testing in isolated environments without external network connectivity before deployment. The aim would be to identify dangerous capabilities and reduce the risk of models being used for large-scale cyberattacks or other catastrophic misuse.
Fifth, verification and international inspection. Khanna argues that an agreement between strategic competitors would require mechanisms to verify compliance. He proposes jointly developed verification technologies, inspection regimes and potentially an international AI inspection agency, drawing on the logic of Cold War arms-control agreements.
The proposal highlights a difficult contradiction at the centre of frontier AI governance. The United States and China regard AI as a source of economic, technological and national-security advantage, creating strong incentives to maintain rapid development.
Some of the risks associated with increasingly autonomous systems are transnational: cyberattacks, biological misuse, model theft, loss of control and failures involving AI-enabled critical infrastructure would not necessarily remain within national borders.
Khanna’s proposal therefore treats AI safety partly as an arms-control problem. Its underlying premise is that competition does not eliminate the possibility of limited cooperation on risks that could harm both competitors. This approach does not resolve the substantial obstacles involved, including mutual distrust, verification, different regulatory systems and disagreements over what constitutes an unacceptable AI capability.
The US–China dialogue on AI competition already creates an initial diplomatic channel; Khanna’s proposal illustrates how that channel could evolve into discussions about concrete constraints on frontier AI development. At the same time, the five pillars remain a congressional proposal, not an agreed US–China policy framework . Their implementation would require agreement on definitions, technical standards, verification mechanisms and enforcement.
The debate on AI competition nevertheless signals a growing recognition that the governance of frontier AI may require forms of international cooperation comparable, in some respects, to earlier efforts to manage technologies with potentially systemic security consequences.

articles.title_orig: Littleton students become junior journalists for World News Day
articles.title_zh: Littleton students become junior journalists for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
The Goddard School of Littleton celebrated World News Day by transforming students into “junior journalists” for a day on Sept. 28
For one day, students at The Goddard School of Littleton became junior journalists.
Wearing ties and carrying cardboard microphones, children interviewed classmates as part of the school’s first World News Day celebration. The activity was designed to encourage curiosity and help students practice asking questions.
“World News Day really ties into our curriculum that focuses on teaching the students how we ask questions,” said Erin Davis, co-owner of The Goddard School of Littleton. “It asks how we can dive a bit deeper and be investigative.”
The Goddard School of Littleton is a private early childhood education program serving infants, toddlers, preschoolers and pre-kindergarten students. Nearly 700 Goddard Schools locations across the country participated in World News Day this year, according to Chas Kurtz, the organization’s senior public relations manager.
“The idea came from a natural connection we saw between young children and journalists: both are constantly asking questions to better understand the world around them,” Kurtz said.
Becoming a “junior journalist” embodies The Goddard School’s Wonder of Learning program, which is an inquiry-based program that employs a STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Math) approach to its curriculum.
“(World News Day) also gave us an opportunity to bring Wonder of Learning to life because inquiry-based learning isn’t simply about arriving at the ‘right’ answer; it's about helping children learn how to think, explore and continue asking questions,” Kurtz said.
In The Goddard School of Littleton’s gym, kids lined up outside the hallway and were granted permission to enter by their teacher one by one. They sat and waited for instruction from their team of teachers — usually a pair or group comprised of a lead and assistant teacher.
On the walls were different stations for the students to explore. One station was a press conference set up with a table and props.
Students took turns sitting at the table and answering questions from their peers, like “How is your day?” and “What are you going to be for Halloween?”
Davis, who runs and owns the Littleton school with her husband, Andrew, said each class had its own lesson plan revolved around journalism.
“Our toddlers had newspaper prints to get that exposure to real-world materials,” Davis said.
Jess Reynolds, one of the directors at the Goddard School of Littleton, helped arrange the gym for World News Day to go beyond lesson planning, Davis said.
“It works because it’s a combination of taking what maybe couldn’t fully come to fruition in a classroom and building a better space for that,” she said of the gym activities.
Two children and Jess Reynolds, a director at the Goddard School of Littleton, sit at the press conference table in the gym on Sept. 28
As the kids rotated between being the interviewer and the interviewee, Reynolds and Davis hopped around different classrooms to help and see what the students were up to. Reynolds, who also works on social media promotion for the school, took videos of two students talking about their weekends and asking each other questions.
“It’s awesome to see what they come up with and see them think through their questions and answers,” she said.
In the class with 2-year-olds, they colored in comics and food illustrations for a food review column.
Other classes had a map of the state with clouds, a sun, and raindrops to experience meteorology reporting.
Asking questions gives children power, Kurtz said.
“Asking ‘why,’ ‘how’ or ‘what if’ is one of the ways children learn to make sense of the world. And when they ask a question, listen to someone else’s perspective, investigate an idea and share what they discover, they’re building skills that extend far beyond journalism,” he said. “They’re learning to think critically, communicate, problem-solve and remain curious.”
According to Davis, helping students grasp the basics of various media forms, ranging from news articles to television programming, is important.
That fundamental principle inspired the creation of World News Day: the belief that journalists bear the responsibility of delivering trustworthy news and information essential to supporting both citizens and a democratic society.
World News Day is celebrated annually on Sept. 28, and The Goddard School may continue its junior journalist trend next year.
“We’ve especially loved seeing the celebration extend beyond the classroom by connecting local media with our students and staff and bringing our wider communities together to celebrate journalism,” Kurtz said. “We’re looking forward to learning from this year’s experience and exploring how we can build on our World News Day celebration in the future.”
Davis said after World News Day wraps up for The Goddard School of Littleton, she would be interested in celebrating again next year.
“One of the great things about our curriculum and our teachers is that we can try new things and grow them every time and focus on adaptability,” she said.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Just Launched 3 Rockets in 13 Hours. Here’s What Investors Need to Know Right Now.
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Just Launched 3 Rockets in 13 Hours. Here’s What Investors Need to Know Right Now.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) just launched three rockets in less than 13 hours, a pretty incredible feat that's led to a 6% bump in the company's stock so far in Friday's trading.
The company sent four astronauts to the International Space Station, carried a batch of commercial payloads into orbit, and launched a classified satellite for U.S. intelligence.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
So, what does all this mean for SpaceX's business and its investors?
First up was NASA's Crew-13 mission. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Florida carrying four astronauts in SpaceX's Dragon capsule on Thursday, Oct. 1. The crew made it to the International Space Station in under eight hours -- the quickest trip there by an American spacecraft ever.
"Yeah, we we got lucky this time," said SpaceX's director of the NASA Science and Dragon programs, Julianna Scheiman, adding, "That's not to say it couldn't happen again, and if we were to put space station in exactly the right spot for the right launch it could be this or even shorter durations, but this is close to the fastest it could be though."
The crew will spend roughly six months aboard the station. The rocket's first-stage booster successfully returned to earth, landed, and will be able to be used once again.
The next flight, Transporter-18, carried 130 commercial payloads into orbit from California, including an AI prototype from Google's Project Suncatcher, a program designed to test the feasibility of space-based data centers.
Of note, the reusable Falcon 9 booster was on its 25th flight.
The final launch used SpaceX's larger Falcon Heavy rocket to carry a classified payload for the National Reconnaissance Office -- the agency responsible for U.S. intelligence satellites.
Obviously, much of the mission was kept under wraps, but it marked Falcon Heavy's first launch for the agency. SpaceX landed both side boosters back in Florida. Its recovered boosters across the day's three launches totaled four.
While the focus of the last 24 hours has been on the company's launch business, as of its most recent quarter, Connectivity , the segment that includes Starlink, remains the real cash cow. The unit brought in $4.3 billion in revenue and $1.7 billion in operating profit.
Space, on the other hand, reported a $542 million operating loss on $962 million in revenue. Of course, that's a bit misleading. When the company sends up Starlink satellites on its own rockets, the Space unit doesn't record revenue from the job. Connectivity marks the launch costs on its balance sheet and spreads the expense over time through depreciation.
The net effect is that Starlink looks much more profitable than it would be on its own, at the cost of making Launch look less so.
Finally, SpaceX's AI unit recorded a $1.3 billion loss on $2.6 billion in sales. The picture here is rapidly shifting, however, with multiple major compute contracts coming online. Deals to rent out its considerable compute power with Anthropic, Alphabet , and other customers could bring in up to $3.4 billion per month once everything is running.
How profitable this compute push turns out to be depends on when the company can deliver on the promised compute and how much it spends doing so. The unit alone spent $15.8 billion in capital expenditures last quarter.

articles.title_orig: Panda diplomacy family tree: Here's every pair loaned to the US by China
articles.title_zh: Panda diplomacy family tree: Here's every pair loaned to the US by China
articles.content_orig:
China first gifted giant pandas to the U.S. in 1972. Now, they are on loan to American zoos.
China first gifted giant pandas to the U.S. in 1972. Now, they are on loan to American zoos.
Zoo Atlanta has two new residents from China.
Giant pandas Fu Shuang, a female panda, and Ping Ping, a male panda, arrived at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on Sunday aboard the FedEx Panda Express. They are the third pair of giant pandas loaned to the U.S. by China as a form of diplomacy over the past two years.
These pandas were sent one day after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met during a state visit.
China first gifted pandas to the U.S. in 1972 following President Richard Nixon's visit to Beijing. First Lady Patricia Nixon mentioned her fondness for giant pandas to Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, and so two giant pandas were gifted to the American people as a form of diplomacy.
Since then, the Chinese government has been loaning pandas to American zoos in exchange for an annual base fee of $1 million for research and conservation.
The Get the Facts Data Team went through the reports of the National Zoo, San Diego Zoo, Memphis Zoo and Zoo Atlanta and created a family tree from the giant panda pairs that were loaned to the U.S. This does not include short-term exhibition loans, such as the giant pandas loaned for the 1984 Olympic Games.
Nine giant panda pairs have been brought to the country since 1972, and around 25 cubs have been born on U.S. soil. Of these cubs, eight did not survive.
Panda cubs are traditionally named around 100 days after birth. Unnamed cubs died before their naming ceremony.

articles.title_orig: The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached 1,197 feet
articles.title_zh: The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached 1,197 feet
articles.content_orig:
The world’s tallest wind turbine has reached its full height in Germany, and its developer says the extra altitude could roughly double its electricity output.
GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall, including its blades. That makes it Germany’s second-tallest structure, behind Berlin’s TV tower. Its rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground.
Winds at higher altitudes are stronger and more consistent, giving the turbine more opportunities to generate electricity. GICON says its design could produce approximately twice as much energy as a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter.
The turbine has a rated capacity of 3.8 megawatts (MW), while future versions are planned to exceed 7 MW. That projected doubling refers to electricity generated over time, rather than a doubling of the turbine’s rated power.
GICON built the project for Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation, or SPRIND. Official commissioning is planned for November, with final work still to be completed.
Getting the turbine that high required a different approach to construction. Instead of relying on a crane capable of reaching the full height, GICON used a telescoping tower. A specialized lifting system raised the inner tower through the surrounding lattice structure, then secured it in its extended position.
“365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.”
The company also wants to use that extra height to get more electricity out of existing wind farms.
GICON and SPRIND envision adding these taller turbines as a “second tier,” with their rotors operating above those of conventional turbines. Their current assessment suggests Germany’s existing wind farms could potentially accommodate up to 4,000 high-altitude turbines, adding generation without developing new wind farm areas.
That’s an estimate of what might be possible, rather than an announced construction pipeline. The Schipkau turbine is still a pilot, and its projected energy yield has yet to be demonstrated in operation.
GICON and SPRIND are now preparing to scale up the design and discussing commercialization with interested wind energy companies. Their goal is to begin series production as quickly as possible. First comes commissioning, and then they’ll see how much electricity the world’s tallest wind turbine actually delivers.

articles.title_orig: Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Data for Lybalvi and Aristada
articles.title_zh: Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Data for Lybalvi and Aristada
articles.content_orig:
Real-world data show Lybalvi cuts acute care visits in schizophrenia or bipolar I with AUD, while long-acting aripiprazole offers flexible dosing and stable symptom control.
Retrospective claims analysis data showed significant reductions in hospital and emergency department visits after initiation of Lybalvi (olanzapine/samidorphan) among patients with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder and comorbid alcohol use disorder (AUD), according to Hemangi Panchmatia, MS. Acute care events were measured in 4 categories: all-cause, mental health–related, disease-related, and AUD-related. "We saw a significant reduction across all of these 4 categories in our schizophrenia patients as well as bipolar I disorder patients who have a comorbid alcohol use disorder," Panchmatia said.
Samidorphan, an opioid antagonist with strong binding at the mu receptor, was combined with olanzapine to attenuate weight gain and metabolic dysfunction. Peripheral effects included glucose metabolism and fat accumulation, whereas central effects on the brain's reward system may have supported satiety and reduced cravings.  Antecedent studies fed into a long-term open-label extension lasting up to 4 years or beyond for many patients, and mitigation of weight gain and metabolic dysfunction was associated with better adherence and longer persistence. 1 Many patients had no significant weight gain, and metabolic parameters remained stable over a long period. Findings extended across schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder and across patients early in illness and those more typical of clinical trials. "It's important to provide your patients with an efficacious treatment that they can adhere to, that they can tolerate, and that they will stay on for long periods of time," McGrory said.
A separate clinician-focused poster summarized the development program for aripiprazole lauroxil, a long-acting injectable prodrug formulated to reduce absorption. This design allowed extended release with consistent, predictable plasma concentrations and without pronounced peak and trough effects, maintaining patients at levels relevant to their symptoms. Dosing once monthly, every 6 weeks, or every 2 months allowed clinicians to individualize intervals. Significant symptom reductions were observed on the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale, with improvement on the Clinical Global Impression–Severity scale. 2 The adverse event profile mirrored that of oral aripiprazole over an extended period, including low sedation and lower levels of metabolic dysfunction and weight gain.
Dr McGrory is medical strategy lead for psychiatry and senior medical director & product lead at Alkermes.
Ms Panchmatia is senior director and head of psychiatry HEOR at Alkermes.
1. Jain R, Penn A, Carbray J, et al. Acute care events following initiation of olanzapine/samidorphan among patients with schizophrenia or bipolar 1 disorder and comorbid alcohol use disorder. Poster presented at: Psych Congress 2026 Annual Meeting; September 15-19; New Orleans, LA. Accessed September 18, 2026.
2. Kempf B, Carbray J, Barbee R, et al. Use of an aripiprazole lauroxil injection administered once every month, 6 weeks, or 2 months in people with schizophrenia: a clinician focused summary of study data. Poster presented at: Psych Congress 2026 Annual Meeting; September 15-19; New Orleans, LA. Accessed September 18, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Fighting Intensifies in Yemen, Raising Fresh Fears of All-Out War
articles.title_zh: Fighting Intensifies in Yemen, Raising Fresh Fears of All-Out War
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels conducted intense attacks across frontlines in Taiz governorate on Thursday, as the Iran-allied group attempts to build on its lighting offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.
Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the frontlines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.
Still, there are few signs that the Saudi-backed government intends to begin a serious counteroffensive against the Houthis in the near future, despite the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi calling for a general mobilisation against the rebels on September 25.
The government instead seems to be pursuing a more gradual process, building up its military forces and attempting to make them more cohesive.
Abdul Basir al-Bahr, a senior official with the internationally recognised government army’s Taiz Military Axis, told Al Jazeera that the general mobilisation call was part of that effort.
Al-Bahr said plans include bringing reserve personnel back into the military’s ranks and retraining them, alongside local anti-Houthi fighters and civilian volunteers.
He stressed that the measures were at an early stage and their battlefield impact could not be judged yet.
In Taiz, Al Jazeera’s field monitoring has found that fighting has continued since early September without any major shifts that can be directly attributed to the general mobilisation.
The picture is similar on other fronts, including the Kahboub Mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and in Lahj, south of Taiz.
Yemeni government field commanders told Al Jazeera the general mobilisation had not yet led to frontline reinforcements.
But that does not mean that military activity has not intensified. On Monday, Colonel Majid al-Nazili, spokesman for the government’s military forces, said the forces had carried out more than 400 strikes over a 24-hour period against the Houthis, causing losses in personnel and equipment.
The ability of the Yemeni government’s military to halt further Houthi advances since the Red Sea reversal appears to reflect a combination of more favourable defensive terrain in the Taiz mountains and Lahj, as well as increased firepower.
The loss of the coastline was aided by weak coordination among anti-Houthi forces, who – despite officially being under one military chain of command – appeared divided and unable to respond quickly to the Houthi advance.
In both Taiz and Lahj – as well as Marib in Yemen’s north – anti-Houthi forces have shown more unity and have years of experience preventing Houthi military advances. Government-aligned forces have also had time to reinforce areas where the Houthis are attempting to advance.
The use of air power is also growing, with government forces reporting hundreds of air, drone, artillery and other strikes targeting Houthi positions and reinforcements in the past few days.
After having seized stretches of the Red Sea coast, the Houthis now need control of the mountainous high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and the roads leading inland to consolidate those gains. Their attempts to take that high ground have so far failed, while the expanded territory has increased the manpower and logistical burden of defending their new positions.
The result, so far, is increasingly a battle over roads and supply lines, with neither side so far able to reproduce the kind of rapid breakthrough seen on the Red Sea coast.
Al Jazeera’s Yemen Editor, Ahmed al-Shalafi, said that the current Houthi attack on Taiz was the result of the group’s desire to secure its coastal gains, as well as an attempt to separate government forces.
He attributed their lack of success so far to a number of reasons.
“When you are talking about Taiz, you’re not just talking about Taiz itself, Taiz is connected to Lahj, Aden, Hodeidah, it has political importance, geographical importance, military importance,” al-Shalafi said.
“There is a difference between the Houthis entering Mocha and between them entering Taiz [city],” he added. “Firstly, the front is strong, there is a cohesion between the tribes and the local forces and the government forces … Secondly, the Houthis do not have a strong base of support in Taiz.”

articles.title_orig: Missouri man adopted as baby learns biological father is rock star Michael McDonald
articles.title_zh: Missouri man adopted as baby learns biological father is rock star Michael McDonald
articles.content_orig:
When Michael Goessling, 59, heard his biological father’s voice for the first time last year, he swore he recognized it.
“I just said: ‘What a voice that guy has!’... it just sounded so familiar, but I couldn’t place it.”
When they spoke over the phone that night, it clicked.
“Finally, I just said: ‘Are you Michael McDonald?’” Goessling recalled. “And he chuckled and he said, ‘Yeah, I’m afraid so.’”
McDonald, a five-time Grammy winner who is lead vocalist of the Doobie Brothers and a successful solo artist, had a child in Missouri with his middle school sweetheart and neighbor when they were 14-years-old, Goessling told NBC News on Friday.
The pair gave up the baby in a closed adoption to Goessling’s parents, who lived roughly 20 minutes away in a suburb of St. Louis, and went their separate ways, Goessling said.
Nearly 58 years later, they reached out to their son.
In May, Goessling said he received a letter in the mail from his biological parents asking to make contact. The 59-year-old said they tracked him down after one of Goessling’s half-brother’s found him through a 23andMe DNA test.
Goessling said he spoke with his biological mother that night and suggested that they get lunch that Friday — a date which had sentimental value.
“She became very emotional and said, ‘Your birthday.’ And I said ‘Yes, you’ve waited long enough. I’ve waited long enough. Let’s meet on my birthday, 58 years to the day,’” he said.
The pair met that Friday, and Goessling got a voice memo from his biological father that night.
Goessling and McDonald spoke over the phone for the first time the following day. Going into the call, Goessling said he knew only his father’s first name.
“I said to Mike, ‘So hey, tell me, what do you do?’ And he said, ‘Well, I’m a musician.’ And I said, ‘That is awesome. I love music. I’ve always been a music nut,’” Goessling said.
Goessling said his biological father told him he had a show in St. Louis on Sept. 4, 2025.
“I was surprised by that statement, having done the math and knowing how old he was,” Goessling said. “Being a touring musician was not what I was expecting.”
He said he figured McDonald was part of some sort of small touring orchestra, until McDonald revealed in passing that he was performing at the Hollywood Casino Amphitheater. When Goessling Googled who was playing at the music hall on the date and saw it was the Doobie Brothers, he pieced his father’s identity together.
“There are still days I wake up, and my first thought is I am coming out of the craziest dream, and it’s been a year and a half,” Goessling said. “I’m still trying to get my head around all of it.”
Goessling has listened to the Doobie Brothers since he was a little boy and remembers when McDonald replaced lead singer and guitarist Tom Johnston in 1975, he said. He said he was 8- or 9-years-old when the switch occurred, and got into an argument with other children about whether or not a song they were listening to was actually one of the band’s.
“They told me, ‘No, they got a new singer. It’s Michael McDonald.’ And I was like, ‘Well, this is awesome,’” he said. “And I was just a fan from the get go.”
Goessling said he’s seen the Doobie Brothers in concert twice before learning McDonald was his biological father.
His adopted family was supportive of his reunification with his biological parents, Goessling said.
For the first time, Goessling’s entire family got together the evening before McDonald’s concert in St. Louis, which he described as “one of the greatest events of my life.”
Goessling said that he later learned his biological parents had made several attempts to reach him in his life with similar letters, but he did not receive them. He said that although his biological parents both dated other people and had other children, they remained good friends over the years.
“I just wanted to thank them for the choices they made on my behalf and for giving me a shot in this world, and how grateful I was for that,” he said. “They were always heroes in my story.”
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos
articles.title_zh: ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — French schools are getting torched. The far right’s brightest star is fighting for his political life after being accused of antisemitic remarks. And economic indicators are flashing bright red to warn of a potential sovereign debt disaster in the country.
The crises that have rocked France in recent days are exacerbating partisan cleavages in the country’s increasingly no-holds-barred presidential campaign.
In the words of one government adviser: “It’s the maxi merde .”
Though that individual, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the current situation, was only referring to the increasingly violent demonstrations outside secondary schools and the government’s slow-footed response to them, it’s a sentiment likely shared by French voters after a week of particularly bleak headlines.
If there are political winners, it’s not immediately clear who they are. Establishment candidates and moderate voices are still struggling to seize the narrative from far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen and her surging far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon — both of whom want to fundamentally reshape France and its relationship with Europe.
A survey by pollster Odoxa this week found that the French disapprove of the government’s handling of the student school protests, but they also disapprove of Mélenchon and his far-left party France Unbowed’s involvement.
Mélenchon’s allies have joined demonstrators outside schools, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police. But the government and France Unbowed’s political opponents accuse them of fanning the flames of violence — allegations they deny.
“There’s a battle over the narrative” between the political extremes, a Socialist Party adviser said.
Whatever the case, the week’s crises are showing just how nasty the campaign can get with two populist candidates unafraid to stoke partisan divisions leading the polls.
The French government has tried to get a grip on the unravelling protests, holding a crisis meeting Thursday and meeting youth representatives on Friday.
“Lecornu is always running behind the crises, he’s always reacting,” said a centrist adviser.
Le Pen, however, blamed agitators for stirring up violence at the protests and accused France Unbowed of “giving a helping hand” to “agents of chaos and insurrection.”
For her National Rally party, the crisis is a useful opportunity to try to convince voters that her party is the best choice for those concerned with public safety.
“We have a government that is incapable of maintaining public order and a left that is stoking the fire,” said National Rally MP Laurent Jacobelli in an interview with POLITICO.
“We are the only legitimate ones when it comes to [security],” he added.
But the unrest is also a useful distraction for Le Pen as her party president and heir apparent, Jordan Bardella, tries to bat down allegations published Monday by investigative outlet Mediapart that he sent antisemitic messages on Facebook Messenger when he was a 17-year-old activist.
Bardella vehemently denied the allegations and vowed to sue Mediapart, but the website on Thursday published another story outlining how it verified the claims, which included screenshots and conversation data downloaded directly from Meta with the help of their sources.
Bardella was tipped to become Le Pen’s prime minister if she came to power, but his future appears to hang on a thread.
“Do we need to unplug him? It’s Marine’s decision,” said a National Rally elected representative. “It all depends on whether the proof is serious.”
But Bardella is no small player, and the National Rally’s opponents are hoping that the fallout of his possible resignation would damage Le Pen’s campaign durably.
All of this comes just hours after Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s minority government introduced a 2027 budget with €43 billion worth of savings designed to reassure markets fretting about France’s massive debt and a stubbornly high budget deficit.
But without a parliamentary majority, getting lawmakers to agree to painful cuts will be tough, even if the specter of a potential financial crisis is starting to loom large.
Borrowing cost have reached their highest levels since 2008 and the spread between French 10-year bonds and German ones — an indicator that measures investors’ appetite to hold French debt over more traditionally stable German debt — shot above 150 basis points on Friday, a level not seen in years.
One lawmaker from President Emmanuel Macron’s party Renaissance said he doesn’t see how the presidential hopefuls from the political center — former PMs Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal — will be spared the fallout.
“Every minute spent on the budget is a minute spent staring at our incapacity to get ourselves out of the mess,” the MP said.
Meanwhile, Mélenchon has called for his party officials to join more protests planned next Tuesday and protect pupils against alleged police violence. That could propel him to center stage, but it could also backfire if he is seen as taking part in the unrest.
Centrist MEP Sandro Gozi said the allegations against Bardella and the far left’s attitude to the protests “complicate the normalization strategy of the two sides.”
“Both Le Pen and Mélenchon are extremists who are far from fundamental Republican and European values,” Gozi said.
But as Macron’s term winds down, a sense is taking hold that France has been mismanaged and that parts of the country are falling apart.
It’s a perception any would-be successor with links to the current president will struggle to combat on the campaign trail.
Elisa Bertholomey and Sarah Paillou contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Cornell 'gang rape' case: Hochul, Letitia James give update after AG appointed special prosecutor
articles.title_zh: Cornell 'gang rape' case: Hochul, Letitia James give update after AG appointed special prosecutor
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK (WABC) -- The Cornell rape accuser was "failed" by people obligated to protect her, including police and the prosecutor, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said at a news conference on Friday.
A visibly outraged Hochul blasted Cornell University Police, the Tompkins County district attorney and the state's rape laws before introducing Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the controversial case
James told a packed news conference at the governor's office that this is now "an active criminal investigation." She pledged a full and fair investigation.
"Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard, that is the promise of our justice system," James said.
Hochul said the system failed Jane Doe. Information from her interview with police was not passed to the district attorney, who then failed to interview her.
"I am deeply disturbed by Cornell University's police and how they handled this," Hochul said. She said sending a "partial record" to the district attorney was a failure.
"In what world would the police learn from the victim that she had literally been gang raped" and that she believed "100%" she had been raped and not elevate those allegations, Hochul said.
Hochul claimed the Tompkins County district attorney then did not do the "bare minimum" and interview the woman after receiving the six-page police report.
"In what world does the district attorney not interview her or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked again. That is "exactly why we're here today and why I took the action last night ."
Tompkins County District Attorney Matt Van Houten told ABC News that CUPD's six-page summary of Jane Doe's allegations convinced him no crime occurred.
Hochul also took the opportunity to call for a change in the state law around voluntary intoxication in cases of sexual assault. She said lawmakers must address this part of the law as soon as possible.
Jane Doe's attorney said he and his client are "pleased" the governor appointed a special prosecutor because "contradictions between the district attorney's statements and those of the Cornell police have been shocking."
Van Houten said Friday he supports the governor's decision to remove him from the case and pledged his cooperation with the attorney general.
Cornell has also endorsed Hochul's decision to remove the DA from the case and assign it to James.
"We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State's rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case," a spokesperson said.

articles.title_orig: Stocks rise after soft jobs data; Nasdaq hits record led by Nvidia: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks rise after soft jobs data; Nasdaq hits record led by Nvidia: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks rose Friday following a surprisingly weak jobs report that raised hopes the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady in October.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 250 points, or 0.5%. The S&P 500 gained 0.7%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.2%, hitting an all-time high earlier in the day before pulling back as Treasury yields reversed course.
Despite Friday's rally, the Dow was down for the week by about 1.3%. The S&P was little changed, off 0.3%, while the Nasdaq was up 0.6% on the week, with Friday marking its third straight advance.
Treasury yields initially fell Friday following the September employment report, but later rebounded, pushing U.S. equities off their highs for the session.
Tech stocks rallied as risk-taking returned on Wall Street, with shares of Nvidia hitting an all-time high for the first time since May, though it closed below its previous record close. CrowdStrike , Palo Alto Networks and AMD also all rose to all-time highs. Shares of AMD also rose nearly 3%.
Last month's nonfarm payrolls report showed the U.S. economy added 29,000 jobs last month, with unemployment rising to 4.2%. The Dow Jones consensus called for jobs growth of 84,000 and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.
"This is the exact kind of number the market wanted from a labor standpoint," said Phil Blancato, chief market strategist at Osaic. "Not too hot, not too cold ... not overly great, and not weakening."
That number made traders reassess the next move for the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 77% likelihood the central bank will stand pat at this month's meeting, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
Saira Malik, chief investment officer at Nuveen, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the report may give the market support before earnings season kicks off, which she thinks will be "very strong."
"So, I think this could be the start of the Santa Claus rally that we've all been hoping for," she said.
Oil prices pulled back , supporting equities, following a report that European nation states are considering a release of strategic fuel reserves following pressure from the Trump administration.
Investors are coming off a modestly higher session Thursday, to start off the month of October. However, the Dow and the S&P 500 were headed for weekly losses amid a global bond rout, while the Nasdaq was the only major average on pace to end the week with gains.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed to this report
The three major averages rose on Friday following softer-than-expected jobs data.
The S&P 500 advanced 0.49% to 7,722.93. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.19% to end at 27,190.86, while the Dow Industrials rose 250.88 points, or 0.49%, to close at 51,177.44.
Friday's rally put the Nasdaq Composite on track for another winning week.
The technology-heavy index jumped more than 1% in Friday trading, bringing its weekly gain to 0.5%. If that holds, it would mark the Nasdaq's third positive week in a row.
The Nasdaq is the only major U.S. stock index on track to finish in the green. The Dow and S&P 500 have slid about 1.2% and 0.2%, respectively, in the period.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average on Friday was pacing to end the week in the red, despite Friday's 0.5% advance.
The blue-chip index as of late Friday trading was down more than 1% for the week. It's the Dow's fourth negative week in the last five, with its positive one in that time period coming last week when it finished up just under 0.3%.
Citi raised its price target on shares of bitcoin treasury firm Strategy to $240 per share from $136 per share, implying about 34% upside potential.
The change reflects a more bullish outlook for bitcoin over the next year and a higher valuation of Strategy's bitcoin holdings as a result, Citi analyst Peter Christiansen said in a note Friday.
The bank also maintained its buy rating on Strategy, though Christiansen noted investors should take a more cautious view of Strategy's valuation due to the company's growing but "dilutive" cash reserve, which could reduce the benefit of its bitcoin holdings.
Strategy shares were up 3% in early morning trading.
Nike shares fell 6% at the open after tanking 10% in the premarket after the global sportswear apparel giant delivered a mixed first quarter of fiscal 2027 that showed its turnaround timeline is further than expected.
The company reported weak trends in its key China market, despite growth in its core North America segment.
While Nike plans $2.5 billion in cost savings by 2031, management said it expects revenues to decline in the high single digits in 2027.
The stock is down 46% for the year.
October marks the fourth birthday of the global bull market, one where the future trajectory is still to the upside, according to UBS.
"Over the past four years, global stock markets have reached one record high after another because corporate earnings are growing faster than most analysts expected. What many initially interpreted as a short-term recovery has proved to be a structural upswing with global reach," Burkhard Varnholt, senior financial market adviser at UBS Switzerland, wrote Friday.
"We therefore see the real story of this bull market as less about prices and more about an economic revival," Varnholt added.
Tesla deliveries in the third quarter beat Wall Street's expectations on Friday, coming at 486,532 versus 461,100 expected.
Deliveries eased from 497,099 in the year-ago period but climbed up from the second quarter's 480,126 delivered vehicles.
Shares were up in morning trading on Friday.
The Grayscale Zcash ETF (ZCSH) is up more than 60% in the past month, bringing its year-to-date gain to about 253%, thanks to renewed interest in privacy as speculative capital this year has rotated into AI.
Zcash (ZEC) itself – up more than 170% this year compared to bitcoin , which is stagnant on the year – was designed to keep users' financial transactions completely private. It launched in 2016, but the privacy narrative eventually faded as privacy coins became a compliance headache for regulators and exchanges.
Crypto's mainstream investment case has become increasingly institutionalized and transparent, while AI has made large-scale financial surveillance and transaction analysis more powerful. The combination of the two has allowed the privacy narrative to gain traction and lead to the launch of the Grayscale Zcash ETF in August.
By comparison, the popular iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) is down about 1% this year and the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index ETF (BITW) , which tracks the 10 largest cryptocurrencies, is down 5%. Meanwhile, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has gained 12% and the Invesco QQQ is up nearly 22%.
Nvidia popped on Friday, briefly hitting an all-time intraday high.
Shares of the semiconductor firm rose more than 3% to as much as $237.88 on the day. At its peak, the stock traded at its highest intraday level ever.
Nvidia's shares began trading on the public market in January 1999.
Revisions in the September jobs report for July and August are making those months look weaker for job creation.
July was marked down by 31,000 to mark a net job loss of 10,000 on the month, the Labor Department reported Friday. August was marked down by 29,000 for a new total of 133,000 compared to the initial robust report of 162,000.
"Revisions made both July and August look weaker, too. Over the past 3 months, we've an average of a mere +17k per month," economist Justin Wolfers wrote on social media .
Stocks opened higher Friday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 322 points, or 0.6%. The S&P 500 gained 0.8%, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.1%.
The latest fed funds futures trading showed an 86% likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady when it convenes for its Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. That's up from a roughly 76% chance just one day prior.

articles.title_orig: Woman at centre of Cornell rape inquiry was 'failed' by officials, says New York governor
articles.title_zh: Woman at centre of Cornell rape inquiry was 'failed' by officials, says New York governor
articles.content_orig:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said the woman at the centre of the Cornell University rape case was "failed" at "every turn".
The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, alleges she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024.
The case was investigated at the time but no charges were laid. It recently reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She has now appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead the case.
This appointment was made after Hochul said she "lost faith" in the local prosecutor's ability to oversee the investigation.
Expressing outrage that local prosecutors did not interview the accuser themselves,  Hochul on Friday said: "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her."
She has also vowed to close a "loophole" that prevents prosecutors from pursuing rape charges in cases when the victim has voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol. Jane Doe is believed to have voluntarily taken drugs and alcohol on the night of the alleged gang rape.
"If someone is too intoxicated to consent it should not matter if they chose to use drugs or alcohol," said Hochul, adding: "Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for gang rape."
James, who is the state's chief legal officer, appeared alongside Hochul at Friday's news conference, pledging to "lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
She said her office would interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted.
District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who previously led the investigation, has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.
In a statement on Friday, he said he supported James' investigation, adding: "It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the university."
Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.
Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.
Speaking to CNN on Friday, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said she is "not doing well".
"She's under siege on social media, where people are trying to identify her; some false court postings, attempting to identify her," he said.
Survivor and victim advocates say current state law on sexual assault makes it difficult for charges to be brought against perpetrators if the victim voluntarily took drugs or drank alcohol before the alleged assault took place.
A bill to address what Hochul described as a legal loophole was already before the state legislature prior to this week's public outcry over how police and investigators handled the Cornell rape allegations.
People who have voluntarily become intoxicated to the point that they are unable to give consent are currently not protected by New York's rape laws, says state assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz, who first sponsored legislation to close the loophole in 2019.
"The real bottom line is that right now if you are voluntarily intoxicated, you will not get justice," he tells BBC News.
"Being voluntarily intoxicated, basically, is almost like giving somebody a get out of jail free card."
Dinowitz says that around half of US states have already changed their laws to say it makes no difference whether intoxication is voluntarily or involuntarily in rape cases.
Hochul said she will support the existing bill and that it could move forward as early as the next legislative session which reconvenes in January. As governor, she could also call lawmakers back for a special session before then.

articles.content_orig:
Russian Egor Kornev equaled the short course world record in the 100m freestyle at the opening stop of the World Aquatics Swimming World Cup.
Kornev, 22, clocked 44.84 seconds in Baku, Azerbaijan, tying the world record set by Australian Kyle Chalmers in October 2021.
The three-stop World Cup is held in short-course (or 25-meter) pools as opposed to 50-meter (long-course) pools used at the Olympics.
Kornev is a recent breakout sprinter. In long course this year, he became the third-fastest man in history in the 100m free and 50m fly and the fifth-fastest ever in the 50m free.
He took silver in the 50m and 100m frees and gold in the 50m butterfly in long course at the European Championships in August.
He was fifth in the 50m and 100m frees in his long-course World Championships debut in 2025.
The World Cup stop in Baku concludes Saturday with finals at 10 a.m. ET, live on Peacock .

articles.title_orig: Spain's government dealt blow after parliament rejects housing measures. Early election speculated
articles.title_zh: Spain's government dealt blow after parliament rejects housing measures. Early election speculated
articles.content_orig:
Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election.
Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home.
The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes.
Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced.
The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament.
Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies.
Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a sharp rent increase introduced by Urbagestión, the company that owned her flat in central Madrid.
Hundreds of protesters gathered to oppose the eviction last week and the case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years.
The social backlash has seen Urbagestión negotiate the return of Abascal to her flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued, with people occupying squares in Madrid and other cities, pitching tents in squares and with a series of marches scheduled for this weekend.
The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation".
Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas .
The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress.
"I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary".
He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society".
Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms.
"Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said.
"Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people."
However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour.
She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve."
The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further.
Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

articles.title_orig: Obama judge halts Trump firing bid as decades-old legal authority tees up possible major reversal
articles.title_zh: Obama judge halts Trump firing bid as decades-old legal authority tees up possible major reversal
articles.content_orig:
U.S. District Court Judge James Boasberg, who blocked President Donald Trump from deporting hundreds of Venezuelan migrants, is among the judges who have attracted attention from critics. 'Fox News @ Night' takes a closer look.
An Obama-appointed judge blocked President Donald Trump from firing court-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Washington Roger Rogoff, ordering the Justice Department to recognize Rogoff as the rightful officeholder and restore his ability to serve.
"This is yet another ruling from an activist judge trying to thwart President Trump’s agenda and undermine his constitutional authority. U.S. attorneys serve at the pleasure of the President," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.
Judge Stanley Bastian, who was first nominated by Obama in 2013, issued a preliminary injunction reinstating Rogoff and barring the administration from treating him as having been lawfully removed. The ruling sets up a legal fight over whether a president can fire a U.S. attorney appointed by federal judges. A 1979 Justice Department opinion and a 2000 federal appeals court ruling both concluded that the president has that authority.
"We disagree with the decision and intend to seek an immediate stay and will appeal," the DOJ Rapid Response account wrote.
TRUMP ADMIN FIRES US ATTORNEY IN SEATTLE MINUTES AFTER HE WAS APPOINTED
President Donald Trump’s administration secured an interim Supreme Court victory allowing it to continue third-country deportations while the legal battle plays out. (Getty Images)
Some legal experts and conservative attorneys took to social media to sharply criticize the ruling, arguing it infringes on the president's constitutional authority over the executive branch.
"Another lawless and dangerous ruling. Violating the separation of powers. By another Democrat activist judge. This time? Seattle Obama Judge Stanley Bastian," wrote Article III founder and president Mike Davis .
"Democrat judges handpicked their own U.S. attorney. The President, through his attorney general, fired him. Under Article II of the Constitution , the President clearly has the executive power to fire Justice Department officials," Davis added.
Davis also noted Bastian’s first name was misspelled in the order, missing the "e" in Stanley.
'ROGUE' OBAMA JUDGE'S SMACKDOWN OF TRUMP ELECTION RULES PROVOKES OMINOUS WARNING FROM WHITE HOUSE DEPUTY
FILE - The majority of the cuts were aimed at Health and Human Services programs. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"The Federal Judge misspelled his own name in his order. That's how you know it's quality legal work," wrote one user.
"Now Judge Bastian created an unnecessary constitutional crisis by essentially ordering a coup at the Justice Department, by ordering the removal of the President’s pick and putting in Bastian’s judicial puppet. The Ninth Circuit must fix this. Or the Supreme Court will have to step in. Again," Davis concluded.
"The President's power to remove U.S. Attorneys must be unfettered consistent with Article II of the Constitution. Judge Stanley Bastian is wrong here to order Rogoff reinstated. I predict Judge Bastian will eventually be reversed, whether at the Ninth Circuit or by the Supreme Court," said Oversight Project litigation vice president Jeff Clark .
WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER
Justice Department lawyers asked a federal judge Friday to dismiss a lawsuit challenging the Anti-Weaponization Fund, arguing Attorney General Todd Blanche formally terminated it Aug. 2. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
"Judicial overreach, plain and simple. The judiciary does not get to run the Executive Branch. Period," said Holtzman Vogel partner Brian Nieves .
In Myers v. United States (1926), which centered on President Woodrow Wilson's firing of a postmaster without Senate consent, the Supreme Court ruled that the president generally has constitutional authority to remove executive branch officers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
More recently, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel concluded in a 1979 opinion that the president’s statutory authority to remove "each United States attorney" also extends to prosecutors appointed by federal judges.
The case is the latest in a string of legal fights over President Trump's U.S. attorney appointments, following similar disputes in New Jersey, Virginia and New York.
A similar dispute unfolded in New Jersey after the administration sought to keep Alina Habba leading the U.S. attorney’s office after her interim term ended. Federal courts ultimately rejected the administration’s effort to maintain her authority, although the judges’ original appointee, Desiree Grace, did not simply take over the office.
Rogoff’s case goes a step further, directly testing whether a president can remove a U.S. attorney appointed by federal judges under the statutory process for filling a vacancy.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.
